This course is about **production operations**: how a fashion business that already has paying clients turns into a workroom that can produce more garments, at a known cost, to a steady standard, without the owner sewing every seam. It assumes you can already cut, sew and price a garment. If you still need those basics, take the Fashion Business Management core course and the tailoring courses first, then come back here.

Every scale-up starts with one honest question: **where do my hours actually go?** Most owners guess, and most guesses are wrong. You may feel you spend your day sewing, but when you write it down you find that buying trims at the market, answering WhatsApp messages and redoing other people's work eat a large share of the week. You cannot plan capacity, hire well or set targets until you know this.

The first scale-up tool is a simple log of where each working hour went.
Step one: the two-week time log

For ten working days, keep a log in a notebook or a note on your phone. Every time you switch task, write the time and the task. Do not judge or tidy it, just record. At the end of each day, add up the hours under a few fixed headings. Use the same headings every day so you can total them later.
**Cutting**: laying out fabric, marking, cutting pieces
**Sewing**: all machine work
**Finishing**: hand stitches, buttons, pressing
**Client time**: consultations, measuring, fittings, collections
**Buying**: trips to the market for fabric, linings, zips, thread
**Admin and messages**: WhatsApp replies, records, chasing payments
**Rework**: unpicking and correcting faults, yours or a helper's

Two weeks is the minimum because one week can be unusual, for example a week with a big wedding delivery. If you have helpers, ask them to log too. Their logs show where they wait for you, which is often the biggest hidden cost in a growing workroom.
Step two: sort owner-only work from transferable work

Look at each heading and ask: **could a trained person do this to my standard, with a written method and a check?** Cutting a complex lace gown for a bride may truly need you for now. Overlocking seams, sewing straight side seams, pressing, buying standard trims from a list and replying to price questions with a ready message usually do not. Mark each heading as owner-only or transferable. Be strict: "they will not do it as well as me" is often true at first, but it is a training problem, not a reason to keep the task forever.
Worked example: Adaeze's two-week log
Adaeze (for example) runs a three-machine workroom in Ibadan with two helpers. She logged 120 working hours over ten days.
Totals: cutting 30 h, sewing 34 h, finishing 10 h, client time 18 h, buying 12 h, admin and messages 16 h. Check: 30 + 34 + 10 + 18 + 12 + 16 = 120 h.
She marks cutting and client time as owner-only for now: 30 + 18 = 48 h, which is 48 ÷ 120 = 40% of her time.
Sewing, finishing, buying and admin are transferable: 34 + 10 + 12 + 16 = 72 h, which is 60% of her time.
Her helpers' logs show they waited for her to cut pieces on most mornings.

Six of every ten hours Adaeze works could be done by someone else. Her real bottleneck is cutting: helpers sit idle until she cuts. Her first scale-up move is to free cutting time, not to buy another machine.

Find your one constraint

A workroom moves at the speed of its slowest step. In operations language this is the **constraint** or **bottleneck**. It may be the owner's cutting time, one overlocker shared by three machinists, the time it takes to get to the market, or clients who arrive late for fittings. Adding machines before you fix the constraint simply adds more idle machines. Write one sentence: "Right now my workroom is limited by ____." Every module in this course gives you tools to widen that point.

Bespoke builds reputation and suits weddings and special events. Made-to-measure is the bridge to scale: the client still gets a fitted garment, but you cut from a proven pattern, so a trained helper can do most of the work. Batch RTW lets you cut many layers at once and sew in a line, which is where production speed comes from. CMT fills idle machine time with work that needs no selling, which is why many growing workrooms take it in quiet months.
Judging a model: contribution per workroom hour

**Contribution** is the selling price minus the materials and other costs that rise with each piece. It is the money left to pay wages, rent and you. Divide it by the workroom hours each piece takes and you get **contribution per workroom hour**. Because hours are the thing you run out of, this number compares models fairly. Include the hit from unsold stock for RTW, because a top that never sells has used materials and hours but earned nothing.

Made-to-measure corporate dress from her standard block: price ₦38,000, materials ₦14,000, 4 hours. Contribution ₦24,000 ÷ 4 = ₦6,000 per hour.

Made-to-measure gives Adaeze the best and safest return per hour. Batch RTW only beats it when nearly every piece sells, so she starts with small runs. CMT pays less per hour but needs no selling, so she uses it to fill gaps, not as her main line.

Three readiness signs before you batch
**Consistency**: two different people in your workroom can make the same style to the same measurements and finish. Test it by giving the same cut pieces to two helpers and comparing.
**Known cost**: you know the true cost of each style, including fabric waste, trims, labour minutes and overhead (Module 2 builds this).
**Cash cover**: you can buy fabric for a batch and wait for sales without missing rent or wages. If not, start with pre-orders or CMT, where the client funds materials.

If one sign is missing, fix it first. Moving into batches without consistency simply multiplies your faults by twenty. Moving without cash cover is how many workrooms end up with a shelf of unsold stock and no money for the next order.

When you are the only maker, the standard lives in your hands and head. To scale, the standard must live on paper and in a reference garment, so that anyone you train can reach it. Garment factories do this with three tools: an **operation breakdown**, a **standard time for each operation**, and an **approved sample**. You can use the same tools in a three-machine workroom.
A woman explaining steps on a board to a learner
Leaders in a workroom transfer skill with written steps, timed targets and a sample to compare against.
The operation breakdown

An **operation** is one task a person does from start to finish at one station, for example "sew both bust darts" or "insert invisible zip". Write every operation for a style in the order the garment is built. Number them. Keep each one small enough that a new helper can learn it in a day or two. This list becomes your training plan, your production plan and the base of your costing.
Timing an operation: from observed time to standard minutes

A **standard minute value (SMV)** is the time a trained worker should need for an operation at a normal pace, including small allowances. Work-study practice builds it in three steps: time the task to get the **observed time**, adjust it for how fast the person worked compared with a normal pace (the **rating**), then add an **allowance** for fatigue, personal needs and small delays.
Choose a trained worker and explain you are timing the task, not judging her.
Use your phone stopwatch. Time the same operation at least five times on real garments.
Average the times. This is the observed time.
Rate her pace: 100% means normal steady pace, 90% means a little slower, 110% a little faster. Multiply the observed time by the rating to get normal time.
Add an allowance, for example 15%, by multiplying by 1.15. Write the result as the standard minutes for that operation.
Worked example: timing an invisible zip
Adaeze (for example) times her helper Chioma inserting invisible zips on shift dresses.
Five timings in minutes: 9.5, 10.2, 9.8, 10.5, 10.0. Total 50.0, so observed time = 50.0 ÷ 5 = 10.0 minutes.
Chioma is careful but a little slow, so Adaeze rates her at 90%. Normal time = 10.0 × 0.90 = 9.0 minutes.
Adaeze adds a 15% allowance: 9.0 × 1.15 = 10.35 minutes.
She rounds to 10 minutes for planning and writes it on the operation sheet.
The zip operation has a standard of about 10 minutes. If a trained helper regularly takes 20, she needs coaching or the method needs fixing.

The golden sample and specification card

A **golden sample** is one garment of each style that you have checked and approved as the standard. Label it with the style code, size, date and your signature, and keep it clean in a bag, not on the rail for sale. With it, keep a **specification card**: a photo or sketch, key finished measurements, seam allowances, stitch type and length, thread colour, trims list and the operation list. When a helper asks "is this right?", the answer is "compare it with the golden sample", not "ask madam".

Each stage has an owner and a clear **done when** rule. The rule stops arguments such as "I thought you had cut it". If a garment fails inspection, it goes back to the stage that caused the fault, and the ticket records why.
The job ticket

A **job ticket** is a small card or sheet that stays with the garment from cutting to delivery. Use a printed template or a ruled page in a ticket book. It carries: ticket number, client first name and phone, style code, size or measurement card number, fabric description, trims, due date, deposit and balance, a row for each stage with initials and date, and inspection result. Clip it to the cut bundle so it moves with the pieces. Keep client phone numbers only on the ticket and your order book, not on public boards.
The job board and WIP limits

A **job board** is a wall board or large paper divided into columns, one per stage. Each order is a sticky note or card with its ticket number and due date. When the garment moves, the card moves. If you prefer your phone, a free board app such as Trello works the same way, and WhatsApp Business labels can tag chats as New order, In progress or Ready.

The key rule comes from kanban, a scheduling method developed at Toyota: **limit work in progress (WIP)**. Decide the most cards allowed in each column, for example no more than 8 garments in Sew at once. When the column is full, nobody cuts more; the cutter helps finish instead. This feels slow at first, but it stops half-made garments piling up, and it shows you immediately where work is stuck.

How long do garments really take? Little's law

Little's law, widely used in manufacturing, links three numbers: **work in progress = throughput × lead time**. Turn it around and **average lead time = work in progress ÷ throughput**. Throughput is how many garments you finish per day. You do not need software: count the cards on your board each morning and count the garments delivered each day for two weeks, then average.
Worked example: why Adaeze's clients wait nine days
Adaeze (for example) counts her board every morning for two weeks.
Average cards between Cut and Inspect: 36 garments.
Average garments finished per working day: 4.
Average time in the workroom = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 working days.

She wants 5 days. Option A: keep throughput at 4 a day and cut WIP to 4 × 5 = 20 garments, by not cutting new work until the Sew column drops. Option B: keep WIP at 36 and raise throughput to 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2 garments a day, which needs more people or hours.
Option A costs nothing. By capping WIP at 20, each garment spends about 5 days inside, clients get dates she can keep, and the same team delivers the same number per day.

Checking a garment only at the end catches faults when they are most expensive to fix: the hem is sewn, the zip is in, the facing is understitched. Production workrooms build quality **into the line** with short checks at each stage. Your Fashion Finishing course covers how to inspect a finished garment in detail; this lesson is about the system around it: where checks happen, how faults are counted and what they cost.

Four quality gates
Quality gates in a fashion workroom
Fabric and trims check
Cut check before sewing
First-piece check per operation
Final inspection before press
Each gate stops a fault from travelling further down the line, where fixing it costs more.

**Fabric and trims check (intake)**: measure the fabric length, look along the whole piece in daylight for holes, shading and print faults, and check zips and buttons match the order. Note problems on the ticket before cutting.

**Cut check**: count pieces against the pattern list, check grain lines and notches, and match the size or measurement card. A cutting error found here costs minutes; found after sewing it can cost the fabric.
**First-piece check**: when a machinist starts an operation on a new style or batch, the first piece is compared with the golden sample before she continues.
**Final inspection**: measurements, symmetry, stitching, finishing and cleanliness, against the specification card, before the final press.
The defect log

Every time a gate finds a fault, write one line in the defect log: date, ticket number, operation, type of fault, who found it and the minutes spent fixing it. Keep fault names fixed, for example uneven hem, zip ripples, wrong size, loose threads, iron shine or stain, skipped stitches. At month end, the **defect rate** is the number of garments with at least one fault divided by the number inspected.
Pareto: fix the vital few first

Pareto analysis sorts causes from most to least frequent and adds a running cumulative percentage. Often a few fault types cause most of the rework, so you fix those first. The split is not always 80/20; it may be 70/30 or 90/10, but the method still shows where to aim.
Worked example: Adaeze's month of defects
Adaeze (for example) inspected 180 garments in a month. 27 had at least one fault.
Defect rate = 27 ÷ 180 = 15%.
Sorted tally: uneven hem 9, zip ripples 7, wrong size 5, loose threads 3, iron shine or stain 2, skipped stitches 1. Check: 9 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 27.
Cumulative share: uneven hem 9 ÷ 27 = 33.3%; plus zips 16 ÷ 27 = 59.3%; plus wrong size 21 ÷ 27 = 77.8%.
Rework took about 25 minutes per faulty garment: 27 × 25 = 675 minutes, or 11.25 hours.
At her workroom cost of about ₦21.60 per minute (you will calculate yours in the next lesson), rework cost 675 × ₦21.60 = ₦14,580 in time alone, before any replaced fabric.

Three fault types cause 77.8% of the rework. Adaeze retrains one machinist on levelling hems, adds a first-piece check for zips, and makes the cut check include a second look at the measurement card. Her target for next month is a defect rate under 8%.

Quality is also safety and trust

A workroom that is scaling has more people, more machines and more extension cables, so safety habits must be written into the SOP, not left to memory. A workroom also holds clients' body measurements, phone numbers and fitting photos. Under the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, personal data should be collected for a clear purpose and kept secure. In practice: keep measurement books locked away, never post a client's photo without her permission, and do not share client lists in staff group chats.
Workroom safety checks to add to your SOP

Do not overload extension boxes with several machines and an iron; spread heavy loads and switch off at the wall at closing. Keep a working fire extinguisher suited to electrical fires near the door and keep exits clear of fabric rolls. Stand irons on their heel, never face down on fabric, and keep cords away from walkways. Change broken needles with the machine switched off, and keep a first aid box stocked.

In a workroom with paid staff, the easiest way to cost labour and overhead fairly is **by the minute**. You already have standard minutes for each style from Module 1. Now you work out what one productive minute of your workroom costs, and multiply. This method also tells you how many garments your team can make in a month, which is the same calculation turned around.
A spool of thread
Thread, zips and interfacing are small costs, but on the costing sheet every one is listed.
Step 1: productive minutes in a month

Start with the paid minutes of all your sewing staff in a month. Then apply an **efficiency** figure: the share of paid time that turns into standard minutes of work. Nobody produces for every paid minute; there are machine stoppages, waiting, training and breaks. Measure your own efficiency by comparing standard minutes produced with paid minutes over a few weeks. A new workroom is often well below 100%.
Step 2: cost per productive minute

Divide monthly staff wages by productive minutes to get **labour cost per minute**. Divide monthly overheads by the same minutes to get **overhead cost per minute**. Overheads include rent, power and fuel, phone and data, machine servicing, and a fair salary for you as manager. Leaving your own salary out makes every price look profitable when it is not.
Worked example: Adaeze's cost per minute
Adaeze (for example) has three machinists. All naira figures are approximate and illustrative.
Paid minutes: 24 days × 8 hours × 60 = 11,520 per person, so 3 × 11,520 = 34,560.
Measured efficiency 75%: 34,560 × 0.75 = 25,920 productive minutes.
Labour cost per minute: ₦255,000 ÷ 25,920 = about ₦9.84.
Overheads: rent ₦60,000, power and fuel ₦70,000, phone and data ₦10,000, servicing ₦15,000, her salary ₦150,000. Total ₦305,000. Overhead per minute: ₦305,000 ÷ 25,920 = about ₦11.77.
Together: ₦9.84 + ₦11.77 = ₦21.61, about ₦21.60 per productive minute.
Every standard minute a garment takes costs Adaeze about ₦21.60 in labour and overhead.
Step 3: the costing sheet

For fabric, use the yardage from your actual lay or marker, plus a waste allowance you have measured from your own offcuts. For trims, list every item. Then add labour and overhead from the SMV. Finally choose a margin. **Margin** is profit as a share of the selling price, so price = total cost ÷ (1 − margin). For a 40% margin, divide cost by 0.6.

Step 4: monthly capacity and utilisation

**Capacity** is productive minutes divided by SMV. If Adaeze made only shift dresses, capacity would be 25,920 ÷ 75 = about 345 dresses a month. Real months have a mix, so add up the standard minutes of your planned orders and compare with productive minutes. That share is **capacity utilisation**.

Once your costs and capacity are known, you can grow through buyers who order many pieces at once: boutiques, schools, churches and mosques, companies, event planners and other fashion brands. These buyers bring volume, but they also ask for lower prices, longer payment times and firm deadlines. This lesson shows how to test each offer against three things you now measure: **cost, cash and capacity**.

Bigger buyers need written terms: price, quantity, deposit, delivery and payment dates.
The four main channels
**Boutique wholesale**: a shop buys your ready-made pieces at a wholesale price and resells at its own retail price. You get volume and exposure; you give up part of the price.
**Consignment**: the boutique displays your pieces and pays you only for what sells, usually after an agreed period. Less selling effort for you, but your stock and cash wait on their shelf.
**Uniform and group contracts**: a school, company or religious group orders many pieces of one or a few styles in a size range, often with a fixed delivery date.
**CMT for other brands**: you cut, make and trim their fabric to their sample for a fee per piece.

Testing an offer: cost, cash, capacity
**Cost**: is the offered price above your total cost per piece from your costing sheet, with enough profit left?
**Cash**: how much do you spend before you are paid, and for how long? Can you pay wages and rent while you wait?
**Capacity**: do the standard minutes fit in your spare minutes this month without breaking promises to existing clients?
Worked example: a boutique wants 30 tops on 60-day credit
A boutique in Abuja (for example) offers Adaeze ₦11,000 each for 30 peplum tops, paying 60 days after delivery. Her costing sheet says each top costs ₦7,468.
Cost: profit per top ₦11,000 − ₦7,468 = ₦3,532. For 30 tops: 30 × ₦3,532 = ₦105,960. The price works.
Cash: fabric and trims per top are ₦5,280 + ₦1,000 = ₦6,280, so she must spend 30 × ₦6,280 = ₦188,400 on materials before any payment, and wait 60 days after delivery for ₦330,000 (30 × ₦11,000).
Capacity: 30 × 55 = 1,650 minutes, well inside her 6,020 spare minutes.
Her counter-offer: same price, 50% deposit on order (₦165,000) and the balance on delivery, or 60-day terms on a first order of 10 pieces only.
The price and capacity are fine; cash is the problem. With a 50% deposit, ₦165,000 arrives before she buys ₦188,400 of materials, so she only funds ₦23,400 herself and is fully paid on delivery.
When the contract is bigger than your spare capacity

Big contracts are where workrooms most often fail, because the owner says yes before checking minutes. Use your standard minutes and productive minutes from Module 2, then choose: split delivery, add overtime that staff agree to, bring in a trusted partner workroom for some operations, or decline politely.
Worked example: 200 school pinafores
A private school (for example) asks Adaeze for 200 pinafores in one month. Her timed SMV for the pinafore is 40 minutes, and she has 6,020 spare minutes next month.
Load: 200 × 40 = 8,000 minutes, which is 1,980 minutes more than her spare 6,020.
Option 1: deliver 150 in month one (150 × 40 = 6,000 minutes) and 50 at the start of month two (50 × 40 = 2,000 minutes).
Option 2: add agreed paid overtime or one temporary machinist trained on the two simplest operations.
She offers the school split delivery: the classes that start first get their pinafores first.
By checking minutes before saying yes, Adaeze gives the school a date she can keep, instead of promising 200 and delivering late.

What happens to faulty pieces, late changes to the design, and spoiled fabric in CMT.

Growing past three or four people changes the owner's job. You spend less time sewing and more time planning, training, checking and paying. Most conflict in Nigerian workrooms comes from things that were never written down: how pay is calculated, who pays for spoiled fabric, what hours are expected in December rush. Decide these before you hire, and write them down.

Piecework is common in garment production worldwide, and it has a known weakness: if the rate per piece is too low, workers must go faster to earn a living, and quality suffers. That is why the rate must be built from timed standard minutes, and why only pieces that pass the quality gate are paid.
Building a fair piece rate

Choose a target day's pay that a trained worker at a normal, steady pace should earn. Make sure it is never below the current national minimum wage when worked out for a month; check the current figure with the Ministry of Labour or a trusted news source, because it changes.
Take the standard minutes of the operation from your operation sheet.
Work out pieces per day at 100% pace: paid minutes per day ÷ standard minutes.
Adjust to an expected pace using your measured efficiency, so an average worker can reach the target.
Piece rate = target day's pay ÷ expected pieces per day.
Worked example: the side-seam-and-hem operation

Adaeze (for example) wants to pay one machinist per piece for closing side seams and hemming peplum tops. The timed standard is 12 minutes. Her target pay for a trained worker is ₦3,600 for an 8-hour day (illustrative).
Pieces per day at 100% pace: 480 ÷ 12 = 40.
Expected pace using her measured 75% efficiency: 40 × 0.75 = 30 pieces.
Piece rate: ₦3,600 ÷ 30 = ₦120 per good piece.
A fast, careful worker at 90%: 36 pieces × ₦120 = ₦4,320 a day. A slower learner at 60%: 24 × ₦120 = ₦2,880, so she keeps the learner on base pay plus training until she reaches the expected pace.
The rate is fair because an average trained worker reaches the target, faster workers earn more, and pay is only for pieces that pass inspection.
Blended pay: a base plus a quality bonus

Many growing workrooms settle on a blend. Each worker gets a fixed monthly base that covers her basic needs and keeps her steady in slow months, plus a small bonus for each good piece above a monthly target. The base protects the worker; the bonus rewards output; the quality gate protects the client. Set the target from your standard minutes so that an average trained worker can pass it in a normal month.
Example of a blended rule (illustrative): base ₦60,000 a month, plus ₦60 for every good piece above 600 good pieces in the month.
A worker who makes 780 good pieces earns a bonus of (780 − 600) × ₦60 = ₦10,800, so ₦60,000 + ₦10,800 = ₦70,800 for the month.
A worker who makes 550 good pieces earns the base of ₦60,000 and gets coaching on her slowest operation, not a deduction.

When a worker is below standard for several weeks, look first at the method and the machine, then at training, and only then at the person. Ask her to show you the operation, compare with the golden sample and the time standard, and agree one change to try for a week. Write down what was agreed. Most underperformance in a workroom comes from unclear instructions, poorly maintained machines or constant switching between tasks, which the owner can fix.

Working hours, breaks, and how overtime is agreed and paid.
Trial period and how training is recognised.
Spoiled fabric: agree a cap on any deduction in writing, and never deduct for faults caused by someone else or by unclear instructions.
Care of machines and tools, safety rules, and client privacy: no photos of client garments or measurement books on personal social media.
Notice period on both sides.
For legal questions, such as contracts or tax and pension duties once you employ more people, ask a lawyer or an accountant. This course does not give legal advice.
Apprentices are not free labour

If you train apprentices, write down what they will learn, by when, any stipend, and their hours. Use your operation list and training wall chart as their learning plan, and sign off each operation as they master it.

Hold a 10-minute **daily huddle** at the job board before machines start: what is due today, which column is full, who covers which operation, any quality fault from yesterday. A team that sees the numbers understands why WIP limits and quality gates matter.
Cross-train for cover
Use your training wall chart to make sure every operation has at least two people signed off. When one machinist is sick during a wedding rush, the line keeps moving.

Why this matters
Scaling starts with facts, not machines
Know where your hours really go
Find which orders feed the business
Name the one constraint holding you back
Put your standard on paper so others can reach it
This module is for a workroom with paying clients that wants to produce more, without the owner sewing every seam.
It starts with one honest question. Where do my hours actually go?
Next, you will see which orders really feed the business.
You will name the one thing that stops your workroom taking more work.
And you will put your standard on paper, so a trained helper can reach it.
Step one
The two-week time log
Log every task switch for 10 working days
Cutting, sewing, finishing, client time
Buying, admin and messages, rework
Mark each heading owner-only or transferable
For 10 working days, write the time and the task every time you switch task. Do not judge it, just record.
Two weeks is the minimum, because one week can be unusual.
Each day, add up the hours under the same headings. Cutting, sewing, finishing, and client time for measuring and fittings.
Then buying, admin and WhatsApp messages, and rework. If you have helpers, ask them to log too. Their logs show where they wait for you.
Now ask of each heading: could a trained person do this to my standard, with a written method and a check?
Be strict. They will not do it as well as me is a training problem, not a reason to keep the task forever.
Worked example
Adaeze's income per owner hour
For example, Adaeze runs a three-machine workroom in Ibadan with two helpers.
Aso-ebi piece, per owner hour
Bespoke outfit, per owner hour
Alteration, per owner hour
Naira figures are approximate and illustrative.
Adaeze logged 120 working hours over 10 days. Only 40% of that time truly needed her. The other 60% could be done by someone else.
Then she grouped 3 months of orders by type and divided income by owner hours. Aso-ebi pieces earned about 6,250 naira per owner hour, because she cuts several at once.
Bespoke outfits brought in the most money in total, but only about 5,000 naira per owner hour.
Alterations paid least, about 3,333 naira per hour. They bring new clients, so she keeps them, but they are the first task to hand to a helper.
Find your constraint
Widen the slow step first
Common mistake
Buying another machine first
More idle machines
Helpers wait for the owner
Better move
Find the slowest step
Free the owner's cutting time
Write: my workroom is limited by...
A workroom moves at the speed of its slowest step, called the constraint or bottleneck.
Adaeze's helpers sat idle most mornings, waiting for her to cut. Another machine would just stand idle too.
So her first move was to free her cutting time.
Write one sentence for your workroom: right now my workroom is limited by, and fill in the gap.
Four production models
Three ways to add to bespoke
Your tested pattern, adjusted to her measurements. About 6,000 naira per hour for Adaeze. The bridge to scale.
A run of one style in set sizes. Fast to cut and sew, but cash is tied up in stock that may not sell.
Cut, make, trim for another brand. Lower fee, no selling. Good for filling quiet weeks.
To compare models, work out contribution per workroom hour: price minus materials, divided by the hours each piece takes.
Made-to-measure gave Adaeze about 6,000 naira per hour, her best and safest return.
A batch of 20 tops earned about 3,313 naira per hour when only 14 sold. So start with small runs and take pre-orders.
CMT paid about 3,727 naira per hour, but needs no selling. Before you batch, check three signs: consistency, known cost, and cash cover.
Make it teachable
Timing one operation
A fast operation done unsafely is not signed off.
Time the same operation 5 times
Average the times: observed time
Multiply by the pace rating
Add the allowance, for example 15%
Sign off after 3 matching pieces in a row
Break each style into small numbered operations, like insert invisible zip. Time a trained worker on your phone stopwatch, at least 5 times.
Adaeze timed Chioma on zips. The 5 times added to 50.0 minutes, so the observed time is 10.0 minutes.
Chioma is careful but a little slow, so Adaeze rated her at 90%. 10.0 times 0.90 gives 9.0 minutes.
Add a 15% allowance for fatigue and small delays. 9.0 times 1.15 is 10.35, so about 10 standard minutes.
Train one operation at a time, and sign it off when the helper makes 3 pieces in a row that match the golden sample.
Show the safe way first. Fingers clear of the needle, machine off before changing needles, scissors closed and put down, irons on their heel and switched off at the wall.
The golden sample
Label it and keep it clean
Style code, size, date, your signature
Kept in a bag, not on the rail for sale
Spec card: measurements, stitch, thread, trims
The operation list with standard minutes
A golden sample is one garment of each style you have approved. Label it, keep it clean in a bag, and keep a specification card beside it.
When a helper asks, is this right, the answer is, compare it with the golden sample, not ask madam.

Why this matters

In this module, every order follows one written path.

And you learn how much work you can promise.
One-page SOP
Six stages, six owners
When a column is full, nobody cuts more.
Intake: style, measurements, deposit, due date
Cut: pieces cut, notched, bundled with ticket
Sew: operations done in order
Finish: hand work, buttons, pressing
Inspect: against the golden sample
Deliver: balance paid, ticket closed
A standard operating procedure, or SOP, is the written way your workroom handles every order, on one page on the wall.
Stage one, intake. Style agreed, fabric checked, deposit paid, due date set.
Stage two, cut. The pieces are cut and bundled with a job ticket that travels with the garment to delivery.
Then sew, in the order of the operation sheet, and finish, with hand work and pressing.
Then inspect against the golden sample, and deliver once the balance is paid. Each stage has an owner and a clear done when rule, which stops arguments.
Put each order on a card on a job board, one column per stage, and set a limit, for example no more than 8 garments in Sew. When the column is full, the cutter helps finish instead.
Little's law
Why clients wait 9 days
Lead time = work in progress ÷ daily throughput
Adaeze: 36 garments ÷ 4 a day = 9 days
Cap work in progress at 20: about 5 days
Set due dates from your board, not from hope
Little's law says average lead time equals work in progress divided by garments finished per day.
Adaeze had about 36 garments inside, and finished 4 a day. 36 divided by 4 is 9 working days.
By not cutting new work until the Sew column dropped, she capped it at 20. Now each garment spends about 5 days inside, at no extra cost.
Set due dates from your board, plus a few days for fittings. A date you keep builds more trust than a fast date you miss.
Quality gates
Four checks along the line
Fabric and trims check at intake
First-piece check for each operation
Final inspection before the press
Checking only at the end catches faults when they cost most to fix. So check at four gates. At intake, look along the fabric in daylight for holes and shading.
Before sewing, count the pieces and check the measurement card. A cutting error found here costs minutes, not the fabric.
When a machinist starts a new style, compare her first piece with the golden sample.
Then a final inspection against the specification card. Write every fault in a defect log with a fixed name.
Pareto
Fix the vital few faults first
33.3% of faults. Adaeze retrains one machinist on levelling hems.
Now 59.3% together. She adds a first-piece check for zips.
Now 77.8% together. The cut check gets a second look at the measurement card.
Adaeze inspected 180 garments in a month and 27 had a fault. That is a defect rate of 15%.
She sorted the faults from most to least. Uneven hems came first, 9 of the 27.
Zip ripples came next, 7 more.
Then wrong size, 5. These three caused 77.8% of the rework, which cost about 14,580 naira in time alone. So she fixes those methods first.
Costing by the minute
What one minute costs you
Paid minutes of all sewing staff
Times your measured efficiency
Wages ÷ productive minutes = labour
Overheads ÷ productive minutes
Include your own manager's salary
Adaeze has 3 machinists, each paid for 11,520 minutes a month. That is 34,560 paid minutes.
Nobody produces every paid minute. At her measured efficiency of 75%, she has 25,920 productive minutes.
Wages of 255,000 naira divided by those minutes is about 9.84 naira a minute for labour.
Overheads of 305,000 naira, including her own salary, give about 11.77 naira a minute. Together, about 21.60 naira for every productive minute.
Leaving your own salary out makes every price look profitable when it is not.
Worked example
Costing a shift dress of 75 minutes
For example, Adaeze costs her shift dress, which takes 75 standard minutes.
Fabric, 1.98 yards with waste
Naira figures are approximate and illustrative.
Here is her costing sheet for one shift dress.
Fabric with a 10% waste allowance is 7,920 naira, and trims, labels and packaging are 1,400.
Labour for 75 minutes is 738 naira, and overhead is 883.
Total cost, 10,941 naira. For a 40% margin, divide cost by 0.6, which gives 18,235. She sets the price at 18,500.
Capacity works the same way: 25,920 minutes divided by 75 is about 345 dresses a month.
Safety and trust
Write these into your SOP
Do not overload extension boxes
Switch off at the wall at closing
Extinguisher for electrical fires, exits clear
Irons on their heel, cords off walkways
Measurement books locked away
No client photo posted without permission
A growing workroom has more machines and cables. Spread heavy loads, switch off at the wall, keep an extinguisher for electrical fires by a clear exit, and stand irons on their heel.
Protect clients too. Lock away measurement books and never post a client's photo without her permission.
Key points
Remember
One-page SOP, job tickets and a WIP limit
Lead time = work in progress ÷ throughput
Four quality gates and a defect log
Plans above 85 to 90% of capacity are a warning
To remember. Use a one-page SOP, job tickets and a work in progress limit. Check at four gates and log every fault. Cost by the minute.
Treat any plan above about 85 to 90% of your productive minutes as a warning.

Growing the business: bulk orders, fair pay and your 90-day plan.
This is the video for module 3 of Fashion Business Management.
Why this matters
Volume brings pressure
Test every bulk offer before you say yes
Pay your team fairly, in writing
Track five numbers and plan 90 days
Boutiques, schools, companies and other brands bring volume. They also ask for lower prices, longer payment times and firm deadlines. So you test every offer first.
As the team grows, most conflict comes from things never written down. So you decide pay and rules before you hire.
And you pull it all into a monthly dashboard and a 90-day plan.
Selling to boutiques
Outright wholesale or consignment
Paid on an agreed date
With outright wholesale, the boutique buys your pieces and owns them. You give up part of the price, but the risk of unsold pieces is theirs.
With consignment, they pay you only for what sells, so your stock and cash wait on their shelf. Start new boutiques small, then move good partners to bigger outright orders.
Test every offer
Cost, cash, capacity
Confirm deposits in your own bank app, not from a screenshot.
Cost: is the price above your total cost?
Cash: what do you spend before you are paid?
Capacity: do the minutes fit your spare time?
A boutique offers Adaeze 11,000 naira each for 30 peplum tops, paid 60 days after delivery. Each top costs her 7,468 naira. The price works, with 3,532 naira profit per top.
But she must spend 188,400 naira on materials first, then wait 60 days. Cash is the problem. So she asks for a 50% deposit of 165,000 naira, and only funds 23,400 herself.
The tops need 1,650 minutes, well inside her 6,020 spare minutes.
Scammers send fake transfer alerts and fake large orders. Confirm every deposit in your own bank or payment app before cutting, and never pay a fee to receive an order.
Bigger than your capacity
200 school pinafores in a month
200 × 40 minutes = 8,000 minutes
Only 6,020 minutes spare
Split: 150 now, 50 at the start of month 2
Or agreed overtime, a partner, or decline
Big contracts are where workrooms most often fail, because the owner says yes before checking minutes. A school asks for 200 pinafores. Each takes 40 minutes, so 8,000 minutes.
Adaeze has only 6,020 spare minutes next month.
So she offers split delivery. 150 in month one, and 50 at the start of month two, for the classes that start later.
Other choices are paid overtime that staff agree to, a trusted partner workroom, or a polite no. A date you can keep beats a promise you break.
Fair piece rate
Build the rate from standard minutes
Pay only for pieces that pass inspection.
Choose a target day's pay: 3,600 naira
480 minutes ÷ 12 standard minutes = 40
At 75% efficiency: 30 pieces a day
3,600 ÷ 30 = 120 naira per good piece
If a piece rate is too low, workers rush and quality suffers. So build it from timed minutes.
Adaeze's target for a trained worker is 3,600 naira for an 8-hour day. Check it is never below the current national minimum wage for a month.
Her side-seam and hem operation takes 12 standard minutes. In 480 minutes, that is 40 pieces at full pace.
At her measured 75% efficiency, an average worker makes 30.
3,600 divided by 30 is 120 naira per good piece. Faster workers earn more, and only pieces that pass inspection are paid.
Blended pay
A base plus a quality bonus
For example, a worker on Adaeze's blended rule makes 780 good pieces in a month.
Monthly base
Bonus: 180 pieces above 600 at 60
Naira figures are illustrative.
Many workrooms blend the two. A fixed base keeps a worker steady in slow months, and a small bonus rewards good pieces above a target.
The base is 60,000 naira a month.
She makes 780 good pieces, 180 above the target of 600. At 60 naira each, her bonus is 10,800.
So she earns 70,800 naira. A worker below target gets the base and coaching, not a deduction.
Write the pay method, hours, overtime, a cap on fabric deductions and notice period into a signed agreement.
Monthly dashboard
Five numbers on one page
Each month, track on-time delivery and your defect rate. Adaeze delivered 187 of 210 on time, and her defects fell from 15% to 8%.
Add utilisation, lead time and margin by style. Read them together. Rising utilisation with rising defects usually means the team is rushing, so slow down intake.
Key points
Remember
Test every offer on cost, cash and capacity
Ask for a deposit that covers materials
Split or decline contracts beyond your minutes
Piece rates come from standard minutes
Hire only when the extra minutes are sold

To remember. Test every offer on cost, cash and capacity, and ask for a deposit that covers materials. Split or decline contracts bigger than your spare minutes. Build piece rates from standard minutes.
And hire another machinist only when the extra minutes are sold.
